titleStmt.title: Integration of Cache Partitioning and Preemption Threshold Scheduling to Improve Schedulability of Hard Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: Integration of Cache Partitioning and Preemption Threshold Scheduling to Improve Schedulability of Hard Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: For preemptive scheduling with shared cache, different tasks may cause interference in the shared cache, leading to Cache-Related Preemption Overhead (CRPD). Cache partitioning is a well-known technique for mitigating unpredictable cache interference in preemptive scheduling, but it reduces cache space available to each task, causing an increase in task execution time. Non-preemptive scheduling algorithms do not incur CRPD, but they generally have poor schedulability. Preemption Threshold Scheduling (PTS) is an effective approach to strike a balance between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling. We propose integration of cache partitioning and PTS to optimize schedulability on a uniprocessor. We force each subset of tasks assigned the same cache partition to be a non-preemptive group, by assigning the same PT to all tasks in the subset that is equal to or higher than the highest priority of the tasks in that subset. This eliminates CRPD within each cache partition, and helps to improve schedulability. We present an ILP formulation as well as an efficient heuristic algorithm.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK
div.p: For preemptive scheduling with shared cache, different tasks may cause interference in the shared cache, leading to increased context-switching overhead. The standard schedulability tests need to be enhanced with analysis of Cache-Related Preemption Overhead (CRPD) [1]. Multiple techniques for CRPD analysis have been proposed, including: ECB-Only (Evicting Cache Block), UCB-Only (Useful Cache Block), UCB-Union, ECB-Union, UCB-Union, ECB-Union Multiset, UCB-Union Multi-set and combined multiset. Non-preemptive scheduling does not incur CRPD, but it generally has poor schedulability compared to preemptive scheduling, especially for uniprocessors.

Cache partitioning is an effective technique for achieve performance isolation among tasks for either uniprocessor or multiprocessor systems. There is a large body of work on cache partitioning mechanisms and policies to improve performance or reduce power consumption for general-purpose computers or large servers, e.g., [2], but we limit our following discussions to related work on hard real-time systems. Cache partitioning can be used to remove inter-task cache conflicts and improve the predictability of real-time multitasking systems, but it comes at a cost: since each task can only use a smaller cache area, which causes increase in intra-task cache related preemption and may lead to larger WCETs and lower schedulability. Cache partitioning can be implemented with either hardware or software. For hardware-implemented cache partitioning, cache partition size is typically coarse-grained, e.g., way-based partitioning, or constrained to be a power of 2 [3]; for software-implemented cache partitioning (either based on compiler techniques [4] or based on virtual memory page coloring [5]), cache partition size can be an arbitrary number of cache sets (as in set-associative cache), but this flexibility comes with the cost of modifying the compiler toolchain (for compiler techniques), or incurring high runtime overhead (for page coloring). Bui et al. [6] considered software-based cache partitioning, and applied genetic algorithm to solve the optimization problem of setting size of each cache partition, and assigning tasks to partitions to minimize system utilization and improve schedulability. Each safety-critical task is assigned its private cache partition, while less critical tasks can share the same cache partition. Estimation of Task WCETs in [6] is based on trace-driven simulation, hence may be unsafe. Lesage et al. [7] presented PRETI (Partitioned REal-TIme shared cache), a hardware-based per-way cache partitioning scheme, which is more flexible and fine-grained that the traditional way-based cache partitioning. Similar to [6], critical tasks are assigned private cache partitions and non-critical tasks can share the same cache partition. Altmeyer et al. [8] presented an optimal algorithm for cache partitioning on a uniprocessor to improve schedulablity of preemptive fixed-priority scheduling, based on exhaustive search with branch-and-bound. They compared two extreme cases: either all tasks share the entire cache, or every task has its own individual cache partition. In this paper, we consider the more general case, where a group of mutually non-preemptive tasks can share the same cache partition. Estimation of task WCETs in [8] is based static analysis with the aiT Timing analyzer [9], which is pessimistic and safe. For multicore processors, Guan et al. [5] presented schedulability tests for global fixed-priority nonpreemptive scheduling on a multicore processor with shared L2 cache, assuming cache partitioning using virtual memory page coloring; Paolieri et al. [10] presented the Interference-Aware Allocation Algorithm (IA 3 ) for joint task and cache partitioning on a multicore processor with partitioned nonpreemptive EDF scheduling; Berna et al. [11] presented Period Driven Partitioning Algorithm (PDPA) for joint task and cache partitioning with consideration of relationships between tasks periods, also for partitioned non-preemptive EDF scheduling, and showed it to outperform IA 3 in terms of schedulability.

There are two broad categories of real-time scheduling algorithms: preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling. For fixed priority scheduling, it is well-known that schedulability of a taskset with non-preemptive scheduling does not imply schedulability with preemptive scheduling, and vice versa. That is, no one algorithm dominates the other in terms of schedulability consistently across all tasksets, although in practice, preemptive scheduling generally outperforms nonpreemptive scheduling. Wang et al. [12] introduced Preemption Threshold Scheduling (PTS), which allows a task to disable preemption from higher priority tasks up to a specified threshold priority; only tasks with priorities higher than the given task's threshold are allowed to preempt it. The designer can control whether two tasks can preempt each other by setting appropriate preemption threshold values. Each task is assigned a regular priority and a Preemption Threshold (PT); a newly arrived task can preempt the running task only when its priority is higher than PT of the running task. PTS is a generalization of preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling: if each task's PT is set to be the highest priority among all task priorities, then it is equivalent to non-preemptive scheduling; if each task's PT is set to be equal to its own priority, then it is equivalent to preemptive scheduling. The benefits of PTS include: minimizing the system stack memory requirement compared to fully-preemptive scheduling, which is important for mass-produced, cost-sensitive embedded systems; reducing the number of runtime task preemptions compared to preemptive scheduling; improving schedulability (with proper setting of priorities and PTs) compared to both preemptive and nonpreemptive scheduling.

There has been a lot work on reducing stack space requirement with PTS ( [13], [14], [15]): two mutually nonpreemptive tasks (threads) can share a common stack space by overlaying the allocation of their stack variables in the shared address space; whereas if one task can preempt another, allocations of their stack variables must be non-overlapping, since the stack variables of the preempted task must be saved and restored when it resumes execution. Therefore, by using PTS to increase the number of mutually non-preemptive task pairs, we can reduce total system stack space requirement compared to fully-preemptive scheduling. In this paper, we exploit another benefit of PTS: a group of non-preemptive tasks can share the same cache partition without causing CRPD overheads. We force each subset of tasks assigned the same cache partition to be a non-preemptive group, by assigning the same PT to all tasks in the subset that is equal to or higher than the highest priority of the tasks in that subset. Since there is no preemption among the subset of tasks assigned to the same cache partition, there is no CRPD among tasks in the same subset; since between different subsets of tasks assigned to different cache partitions do not share cache, there is no CRPD between different subsets. Hence we have eliminated CRPD with this combination of PTS and cache partitioning.

The optimization problem consists of two sub-problems: how to partition the cache and how to assign tasks to cache partitions. We impose the rule that all tasks with the same PT value must share the same cache partition, or equivalently, each PT value uniquely identifies a cache partition as well as the subset of tasks assigned to it. If two different subsets of tasks assigned to two different cache partitions share the same PT value, then we can merge the two subsets of tasks to form a large non-preemptive group, and assign the combined subset of tasks to a larger cache partition by merging the two original cache partitions. This can only help to improve schedulability, since each task now has a larger cache partition size. Given this rule, PT assignment implicitly determines the task-to-cache partition assignment, hence we do not need to explicitly model task-to-cache partition assignment. Combined with size information of each cache partition, the result is a full solution.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows: we present the system model and a motivational example in Section II; background knowledge on Preemption Threshold Scheduling and its schedulability analysis in Section III; the ILP formulation for cache partitioning and PT assignment in Section IV; present the heuristic algorithm in Section V; performance evaluation in Section VI; conclusions in Section VII.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND MOTIVATIONAL EXAMPLE
div.p: We consider the target architecture with a single-level L1 cache with total cache size of T CS cache sets. For directmapped cache, each cache set contains only one cache line; for n-way set-associative cache, each cache set contains n cache lines. We treat each cache set as the minimum unit of cache partitioning, so the size of each cache set is not relevant, and our techniques can be applied to either direct-mapped or setassociative cache equally well.
We consider a task-set Γ = {τ i |1 ≤ i ≤ N } containing N sporadic tasks scheduled by fixed-priority scheduling on a uniprocessor platform.

div.p: We have two choices of cache partitioning: either let the 2 tasks share the entire cache (2 cache sets), or allocate each cache set to one task. For fully-preemptive scheduling, we can show that neither choice makes the task-set schedulable. If each task is allocated 1 cache set, then the total CPU utilization is (3/4+3/4)>1, hence the task-set is non-schedulable; if both tasks share the entire cache, then the total CPU utilization is (2/4+2/4)=1 without considering CRPD; but if CRPD is taken into account, then the total CPU utilization exceeds 1 by a small amount, rendering the task-set non-schedulable. With PTS, if we assign τ 2 PT π 2 = p 1 = 2, then the two tasks are mutually non-preemptive, the total CPU utilization is (2/4+2/4)=1; in addition, since CRPD is 0 for non-preemptive scheduling, the WCRT of both tasks are 4, so the task-set is schedulable.

div.head: III. PREEMPTION THRESHOLD SCHEDULING AND ITS SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: We describe the scheduling rules of PTS: when a task τ i is released, it is inserted into the ready queue with its priority P i . When the task is dispatched at runtime, its priority is effectively raised to its preemption threshold π i and it keeps this priority until the execution is finished. In other words, the currently-executing task τ i can only be preempted by another task τ j if P j > π i . PTS can be viewed as a technique for controlling the degree of preemption, with fully-preemptive and fully-nonpreemptive scheduling as its special cases. If each task's preemption threshold is set to be equal to its priority, i.e., π i = P i , then PTS becomes preemptive scheduling; if each task's preemption threshold is set to infinity, i.e., π i = ∞, or equivalently, equal to the highest priority among all tasks in the task-set, then PTS becomes non-preemptive scheduling. Figure 2 shows an example task-set with four tasks in decreasing priority order τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 4 . Figure 2(a) shows fixedpriority fully preemptive scheduling; Figure 2(b) shows Preemption Threshold Scheduling, where each dotted arrow's endpoint indicates the corresponding task's PT. For each pair of tasks τ i and τ j , we use τ i τ j to denote that τ i can preempt τ j after τ j has started execution. The preemption relation is transitive, i.e., if τ i τ j and τ j τ k , then τ i τ k . Figure 2(c) shows the preemption graph for the PT assignment in Figure 2(b), where each task is represented by a vertex, and an edge from τ i to τ j means τ i τ j . There is no edge from τ 1 to τ 2 , or from τ 3 to τ 4 due to the PT assignment, meaning that τ 1 and τ 2 (τ 3 to τ 4 ) are mutually non-preemptive.

Wang et al. [12] presented the original schedulability analysis for PTS, but it contained minor errors. Regehr [16] presented the corrected version of the analysis, which is used here. The analysis uses the concept of level-i busy period, and checks schedulability of all jobs of each task in the busy period. (Since we are not yet concerned with cache partitioning at this point, we omit the subscript k in the task τ i 's WCET C i,k , and simply use C i to denote its WCET.) Definition 1: (Level-i Busy Period [17]) A time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) during which tasks, of priority i or higher, that were released at the start of the busy period at t 1 , or during the busy period but strictly before its end at t 2 , are either executing or ready to execute. The subset of tasks with higher priority than task τ i is denoted hp(i) = {τ j |P j > P i }; the subset of tasks with priority higher than the preemption threshold of τ i is denoted as ht(i) = {τ j |P j > π i }; the subset of tasks that can cause blocking to task τ i is {τ j |P j < P i ≤ π j }, i.e. tasks with priority lower than P i and preemption threshold higher than or equal to P i .

div.p: Schedulability constraints. For schedulability analysis of preemption threshold scheduling (Section III), we need to check the schedulability of all jobs in the level-i busy period, which depends on task WCETs, which in turn depends on cache partitioning, which in turn depends on preemption threshold assignment, since each preemption threshold value uniquely identifies a cache partition. To break this circular dependency, we use an optimistic ILP formulation to check schedulability of only the first job of each task, as proposed in [18]. This obviates the need to compute the level-i busy period, but also makes the analysis unsafe and may produce false negative solutions that are actually unschedulable, since other jobs in the level-i busy period may miss deadlines. This also makes the ILP solution not necessarily optimal in this paper, in contrast to the usual claims of optimality of the ILP approach.

To reject any false negative solutions, we always run the full PTS schedulability test (Equations ( 1)-( 5)) to confirm the schedulability of solutions found by the ILP model. In practice, we find that only about very small fraction of cases turn out to be false negatives (generally less than 1%).

V. HEURISTIC ALGORITHM FOR CACHE PARTITIONING AND PT ASSIGNMENT We present an efficient heuristic algorithm that is scalable to large problem sizes. It depends on a simplified version of the ILP formulation, described as follows: If each task's cache partition size cps i is known, that is, all the 0-1 variables a i,k become known constants, we can omit Equations ( 6) and (7) concerning the variables a i,k . The rest of the ILP constraints (Equations ( 8) to ( 19)) stay the same except substituting the actual values of the variables a i,k . This simplified ILP formulation is called ILP-heu, since it is used within the heuristic Algorithm 1. It is much more efficient than the original ILP formulation with a i,k as variables.

The heuristic algorithm tries to assign a cache partition size to each task, then invoke ILP-heu to try to assign a PT value to each task. (Recall that each PT value uniquely identifies a cache partition as well as the subset of tasks assigned to it, hence PT assignment implicitly determines the task-to-cache partition assignment.) If a schedulable solution is found, then return the current cache partitioning and PT assignment as a valid solution; otherwise, choose a task and increase its cache partition size to the next larger value, and invoke ILP-heu again.

• Lines 1-3: Initially, assign each task the minimum cache partition size of 1 cache set. • Lines 5-23: The main loop that tries to increase each task's cache partition size to the next larger size until a schedulable solution has been found, or all tasks have been assigned the Total Cache Size. • Lines 6-12: Invoke ILP-heu to try to find a feasible PT assignment. Similar to the ILP formulation in Section IV, ILP-heu only checks schedulability of the first job of each task in the busy period, so it is optimistic and unsafe, and we need to run the conventional PTS schedulability test (PTSSchedTest) to confirm schedulability of the task-set based on current cache partition size and PT assignment. Also similar to Section IV, we ask the ILP solver to return the first solution found, instead of multiple feasible solutions. • Lines 13-15: If every task's assigned cache partition size has reached the total cache size T CS and the task-set is still not schedulable, then return failure.

div.p: • Lines 16-22: Choose a task τ i to increase its cache partition size cps i from CS k to CS k+1 (if it has not reached the maximum value of T CS), which reduces its WCET and improves its own schedulability as well as schedulability of lower priority tasks. Choice of task τ i is to maximize the number of additional tasks that become schedulable due to the increase in τ i 's cache partition size, denoted Δ i , based on fixed-priority schedulability test (FPSchedTest). (This is a simple heuristic that is shown to work well, but it is certainly possible to devise more sophisticated heuristics.) Save the task whose cache partition is selected to be increased as Selected pre , and avoid selecting the same task in the next iteration. Our experience shows that this helps to improve algorithm performance significantly.

div.head: A. Running the Heuristic Algorithm on the Toy Example
div.p: We show the steps of running the heuristic algorithm on the toy example shown in Table I.
div.formula: 1) Initialize cps 1 = cps 2 = 1. Task WCETs are C 1,1 = C 2,1 = 3.
div.p: 2) Invoke ILP-heu, which cannot find a feasible PT assignment. Only the higher-priority τ 2 is schedulable.

3) Try to increase the higher-priority task τ 2 's cache partition size cps 2 from 1 to 2, now C 2,2 = 2. Invoke FPSchedTest to get Δ 2 = NST (cps 2 = 2)-NST (cps 2 = 1) = 1-1 = 0, i.e., it is not helpful to increase τ 1 's cache partition size, since still only the higher-priority τ 2 is schedulable. 4) Try to increase the lower-priority task τ 1 's cache partition size cps 1 from 1 to 2, now C 1,2 = 2. Invoke FPSchedTest to get Δ 1 = NST (cps 1 = 2)-NST (cps 1 = 1) = 1-1 = 0, i.e., it is not helpful to increase τ 1 's cache partition size, since again only the higher-priority τ 2 is schedulable. 5) Since Δ 1 = Δ 2 = 0, choose the higher priority task τ 2 to increase its cache partition size cps 2 = 2, now C 2,2 = 2. 6) Invoke ILP-heu, which cannot find a feasible PT assignment. Only the higher-priority τ 2 is schedulable. 7) Try to increase τ 1 's cache partition size cps

div.head: VI. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: We consider a uni-processor with Harvard architecture (separate instruction cache and data cache), and focus on cache partitioning of either instruction cache or data cache, by considering either instruction cache with perfect data cache, or data cache with perfect instruction cache, same as [8]. Each cache (instruction or data) is a directed mapped cache with total size of 4kB; each cache line has size of 16 bytes. Although the problem formulation is general, we consider hardware-based cache partitioning in our performance experiments, where each cache partition size is a power of 2, so the legal cache partition sizes are {1, 2, 4, . . . , 256}. We consider the following approaches for performance evaluation:

1) Fully-Preemptive Scheduling (FPS). As a baseline for comparison, we consider ideal fixed-priority Fully-Preemptive Scheduling with no cache partitioning, where all tasks share the entire cache space (either instruction or data), and CRPD is assumed to be zero. 2) Non-Preemptive Scheduling (NPS). Since non-preemptive scheduling does not incur CRPD, cache partitioning is useless, and all tasks share the entire cache space (either instruction or data). 3) FPS-BnB the B&B approach proposed in [8], which exhaustively search the cache configuration for each task. 4) PTS-ILP, the ILP formulation proposed in Section IV. To make sure that it produces a truly schedulable configuration, schedulability test showed in Section III is invoked to recheck the schedulability after the task-sets passing the ILP. 5) PTS-Heu, the heuristic algorithm proposed in Section V.

[8] considered several other approaches, including Fully-Preemptive Scheduling with no cache partitioning combined with either sequential task layout or optimal task layout (for reducing CRPD), and concluded that cache partitioning is advantageous in some scenarios but detrimental in others.

In this paper, we focus on comparisons between cache partitioning with FPS vs. PTS, hence we omit the cases of Fully-Preemptive Scheduling with no cache partitioning while considering CRPD. That is, for all of the approaches we consider, there is no CRPD, hence we do not need to consider task layout issues.

The experiment platform is: AMD Athlon II X4 631 Quad-Core Processor with 7.8GB main memory, running 64bit Ubuntu Linux Release 12.04. The IBM ILOG CPLEX Optimizer V12.6.1 is used as the ILP solver. As usual, we use the ratio of schedulable task-sets as the performance metric.

The synthetic task-sets are generated based on the following rules: Task-set utilization is varied from 0.2 to 1 in steps of 0.05; for each utilization value, 1000 task-sets are randomly generated; For a given task-set, each task's utilization is generated using UUnifast [19] algorithm; Task periods were generated according to a log-uniform distribution within the interval [5,5000] ms; Task priorities are assigned rate monotonically; Task deadlines are implicit, i.e., equal to their periods; Task base WCETs, evaluated for the case of being allocated the whole cache, are set based on utilization and period:
div.formula: C i,K = U i • T i .
div.p: Figures 1 and2 in [8] plotted task WCETs vs. cache partition size for programs from the well-known PapaBench [20] and the Malardalen benchmark suites [21], using the aiT Timing analyzer [9] to compute WCET bounds. Instead of performing WCET analysis by ourselves, we randomly select a benchmark program from Figures 1 and2 in [8], which show how task WCETs vary with instruction or data cache size, and use its over-approximation of WCET function depending on cache size to generate task WCETs for other cache partition sizes, using the base WCET C i,K as the starting point.

Figure 4 shows experimental results for task-set size N = 5. For partitioning of either instruction cache or data cache, Figures 4(a) and 4(c) shows that both PTS-ILP and PTS-heu outperforms FPS-BnB significantly, especially if total utilization is high. Figures 4(b) and 4(d) show that PTS-ILP and PTS-heu do not strictly dominate FPS-BnB, i.e., there are some task-sets that are schedulable with PTS-ILP or PTS-heu, but not with FPS-BnB, and vice versa, but the first case is more common, confirming the superiority of PTS over FPS. Figure 4(c) shows that for data cache partitioning, PTS-ILP and PTS-heu even outperforms FPS, the idealized baseline case where all tasks share the entire cache space, even with CRPD assumed to be zero. This is consistent with the fact that FPS and NPS are both special cases of PTS, hence it is possible for PTS to outperform both FPS and NPS with proper setting of priorities and PTs, although this is not guaranteed. To explain why PTS-ILP and PTS-heu even outperforms FPS for data cache partitioning, but not for instruction cache partitioning, we offer the following plausible explanation: as shown in Figures 1 and2 in [8], task WCETs are more sensitive to instructive cache size than to data cache size, i.e., reducing instruction cache size causes a more significant increase in task WCET than reducing data cache size by a similar percentage. We believe this may be due to programs With task-set size of 10, PTS-ILP becomes slower, e.g., it needs 5 minutes on average to process each task-set. Therefore, we perform evaluation for task-set size N = 10 without PTS-ILP. Figure 5 shows similar results as Figure 4.

With task-set size of 20, Figures 6(a) and 6(b) show the results for instruction cache partitioning with perfect data cache. (The results for data cache partitioning with perfect instruction cache are similar to the results for 5 and 10 tasks, and omitted due to space limitations.) It is interesting to see that Non-Preemptive Scheduling (NPS) sometimes outperforms FPS-BnB when utilization exceeds 0.7. Figure 6(c) shows the algorithm running time (in hours) for each taskset. The running time of FPS-BnB can go up to 9+ hours for each task-set if the total utilization is around 0.6, but it is generally quite short for either lower or higher utilizations. To finish the experiments in reasonable amount of time, we reduced the number of cases that are evaluated with FPS-BnB: for each utilization value in the range [0.5, 0.8], 100 task-sets are randomly generated instead of 1000 task-sets for the ranges [0.2, 0.5) and (0.8, 1]. The heuristic algorithm is consistently very efficient, taking at most a few seconds for each task-set.

Comparing the results for task-set with sizes 5, 10 and 20, we can see that PTS-heu outperforms FPS-BnB by a larger margin when the task-set size is larger. In general, larger task-set size gives more freedom for forming non-preemptive groups of tasks, which in turn gives PTS-based approaches more advantage over the FPS-based approach.

In addition to synthetic task-sets, we consider two industrial case studies. The first one from [22] is a task-set of 42 tasks; The second one from [23] is a fuel injection embedded controller, consisting of 90 Simulink function blocks. We assume that each function block is mapped to a real-time task, so the task-set has 90 tasks. Since the two case studies are for allocation on a multiprocessor platform, the task-set utilization exceeds 1 for both cases, we scaled each task's base WCET so that the total utilization is 0.8. Task WCETs for other cache partition sizes are generated using the base WCET as before. For the first case study, it took the heuristic algorithm 30 seconds to find a feasible solution of cache partitioning and preemption threshold assignment; for the second case study, it took 1.5 hours. For both case studies, FPS-BnB ran for days without finishing.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed integration of Preemption Threshold Scheduling with cache partitioning on a uniprocessor platform, and shown its advantages in improving schedulability compared to fully-preemptive scheduling with shared cache and per-task cache partitioning. Possible future work includes addressing other common scheduling algorithms such as Earliest Deadline First (EDF).
